messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Electrician
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 78

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Time of Day: The same time of day the event occurred, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hopelessness: I have no future, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mika had been working as an electrician on a commercial job when the assault happened, finishing up late in the day after most people had already left. He was 42, a Pacific Islander man living in the United States with his partner, and he still located the event in his mind by the hour it occurred, as if the late-afternoon light itself had become dangerous. He remembered being near a doorway when the situation turned. What stayed with him were not smooth, complete memories but a handful of hard, frozen images: the door moving, the sound of it slamming or opening abruptly, a body too close to his, a sudden shift in someone’s movement that told him he was not safe. Between those images there were blanks he could not fill in. He said it was like having only a few pictures from something that should have been a full scene, and the missing parts troubled him as much as the pictures he did have.

In the weeks afterward, Mika found that when the same time of day came around, his body seemed to know before he did. Late afternoon would arrive and he would feel himself becoming unreal, as though he were no longer fully in the room. If a door opened sharply at a job site or slammed somewhere in the building, he was immediately back inside those snapshots, not in the sense of a full recollection but in the way his whole attention narrowed around the sound. He began reacting to sudden movement near him as if he were about to be hit again. A coworker stepping unexpectedly around a corner, someone crossing behind him in a narrow hallway, even his partner moving quickly into the kitchen beside him could make him jolt hard. Unexpected touch was worse. If someone put a hand on his shoulder without warning, he reacted with open alarm before he could orient himself.

As an electrician, he worked in spaces where doors opened without warning and people moved around him in close quarters, often in buildings he did not know well. He began dreading unfamiliar sites because he could not quickly judge exits, sightlines, or who might come through a door behind him. He would ask to stay on jobs he already knew, or linger near areas that felt easier to scan. When he had to enter a new building, he was tense from the moment he arrived. The strain showed at work: he was more irritable, less focused, and increasingly preoccupied with where other people were in relation to him.

At home, Mika tried hard not to think about the assault. He spent long stretches on his phone, scrolling late into the night, or disappeared into games and the internet until he was exhausted enough to sleep. He drank as a way of dulling the edge of the evening, especially when the hour of the assault approached. He also began avoiding television shows, films, or news stories that might involve violence or assault; if something unexpected came on, he shut it off or left the room. These habits narrowed his life over months. His partner saw more of his bent head lit by a screen than his face, and evenings became quiet and disconnected. He was physically present but hard to reach.

When the memory did come, guilt came with it immediately. Because he could not account for every moment, he filled the gaps with self-accusation. He had come to believe the assault said something fundamental about him: that it had happened because of the kind of person he was, because he had failed some basic test that another man would have passed. He compared himself relentlessly to an imagined stronger, smarter person who would not have ended up in that situation. What frightened him most was not only the memory itself but what he took it to mean—that his future had somehow closed down at that doorway too. He described a sense that there was nothing ahead except more vigilance, more shame, more shrinking of his world.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become difficult to hide. He was avoiding unfamiliar work settings when he could, startling at coworkers’ movements, and drinking more in the evenings. His partner had begun commenting on how absent he seemed and how sharply he reacted to being touched. What finally brought him in was a recent moment on a job when a door slammed behind him near the same time of day as the assault, and he felt detached from himself so suddenly that he had to step away and sit in his truck. He said he was afraid that this was who he was now—someone weak, watchful, and finished—but he was also hoping, carefully, that talking might help him understand the missing pieces and let him feel present in his own life again.
